description: We are students and enthusiasts of science and technology from Côte d’Ivoire, with a particular interest in artificial intelligence, software development, data, and digital design. Our training in a preparatory program in mathematics and physics has given us a solid foundation in mathematics, problem-solving, and analytical thinking.
summary: On a long-duration mission, nobody can watch over the crew: there is no doctor on board, and the signal takes tens of minutes to reach Earth. The astronauts therefore carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health. A dashboard that just scrolls does not answer that question. GlobalAstro Health is a decision-support system built around a single question: when does a result deserve the attention of the crew, or of the flight surgeons? It equips both ends of the mission. On board, seven screens let the crew spot a drift on their own: indicators, bones and heart, mental health, radiation, alerts, offline mode, received instructions. On the ground, four screens give the flight surgeon the state of the crew and the full life cycle of an instruction, from preparation to acknowledgement. The five hazards documented by NASA's Human Research Program shape the interface.
details:
GlobalAstro Health is a decision-support system for astronaut health on long-duration missions. It answers one question: when does a measurement deserve action, when there is no doctor on board and the link to Earth is tens of minutes behind?

What it does. The system serves two roles with two different interfaces. On board, the crew gets seven screens: a dashboard where every indicator carries its pre-flight reference and its trend; bones and heart; mental health; radiation expressed as a share of the career limit, never as an absolute dose; alerts that name the deviation, what to do about it, and the corrective action to confirm; an offline mode; and the instructions received from the ground. On the ground, the flight surgeon gets four views: the crew with the values received at the last communication window, alerts derived automatically from out-of-range measurements, the measurement log, and the full life cycle of an instruction — queued, delivered on board, read by the crew.

How it works. On board, fifteen sensors produce twenty-five physiological and environmental parameters. They feed a central module written in Python with no external dependency, which computes thresholds, assigns a status and keeps the local history. Nothing in that chain needs the network: an on-board tool that depends on a link fails exactly when it is needed. Measurements leave at the communication window, which is why the ground interface never offers live action — it prepares, the crew applies, and the acknowledgement travels back at the next window. On the ground, a hosted PostgreSQL database carries the accounts, the instructions and the measurements received.

How we built it. The backend — the Python central module, the sensor layer and the data model — was written by our team. The frontend — the two web interfaces — was built with an AI development agent, under our review and our decisions: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, embedded fonts, and no charting library, since the curves are drawn in SVG. The ground database runs on PostgreSQL. No NASA branding or design element was generated or used.

Impact. The same need exists beyond Mars: Artemis missions, analog habitats, and any setting where a patient is far from a specialist. We also considered what the system must not do — it never automates a medical decision, and every displayed value states its origin, because the measurements here are simulated.

Creativity. The creativity is not in adding one more sensor, but in treating the delay as a design constraint: the communication window shapes the interface, the two roles, and what each side is allowed to do.
